---
title: "4. Binomial Small (n = 5, p = 0.10)"
subtitle: "Skewed AND lumpy: two problems at once"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/clt_helpers.R")
size <- 5; prob <- 0.10
gen_binom <- function(k) rbinom(k, size = size, prob = prob)
```

## What population am I sampling from?

Each observation is the number of successes in 5 trials with success probability 0.10, from `rbinom(size = 5, prob = 0.1)`. One heads-up on notation: the binomial's "$n = 5$" is the number of **trials inside one observation**. It's not my sample size. I'll call the binomial parameter `size` so I don't mix them up.

This population is **highly discrete** (values 0 to 5, but really almost always 0 or 1) and **right-skewed**: 59% of the time the value is 0.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig-height: 4
plot_population(gen_binom, "Population: Binomial(size = 5, p = 0.10)", discrete = TRUE)
round(dbinom(0:5, size, prob), 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: theory
mu    <- size * prob                              # 0.5
sigma <- sqrt(size * prob * (1 - prob))           # sqrt(0.45)
g1    <- (1 - 2 * prob) / sigma                   # skewness
g2    <- (1 - 6 * prob * (1 - prob)) / sigma^2    # excess kurtosis
data.frame(mean = mu, sd = sigma, skewness = g1, excess_kurtosis = g2)
```

## What did I expect?

The skewness is `r round(g1, 3)`, smaller than the exponential's 2, so based on skewness alone it should converge faster than the exponential:

```{r}
predicted_n(g1, g2)
```

So my theory-only guess is about $n = 23$. But I expect the discreteness to slow things down, because the mean of $n$ observations can only be a multiple of $1/n$, and most of the probability is piled up on a few values. My real guess is somewhere between 25 and 60.

## Which sample sizes did I investigate?

The standard grid from 1 to 500, with $B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")`$ repetitions at each $n$.

## Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulate
sweep  <- run_sweep(function(n) simulate_means(gen_binom, n, B), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
tab    <- sweep$table
n_star <- chosen_n(tab)
show_table(tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: pictures
#| fig-height: 12
plot_sampling(sweep, c(1, 5, 30, n_star), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
```

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_convergence(tab)
```

## Theory vs. simulation

- **Mean:** all simulated means are within `r round(max(abs(tab$sim_mean - mu)), 3)` of 0.5.
- **Standard error:** simulated SE / $(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ ranged from `r round(min(tab$se_ratio), 3)` to `r round(max(tab$se_ratio), 3)`.
- **Shape:** skewness first drops below 0.25 at $n = `r min(tab$n[abs(tab$skewness) < skew_cut])`$, close to the theory prediction of `r predicted_n(g1, g2)$prediction`.

## When is it approximately normal?

$$
\boxed{n = `r n_star`}
$$

This is a lot bigger than the skewness-only prediction. Looking at the table, skewness and kurtosis were both fine by around $n = 30$, but the **Q-Q correlation** didn't stay above 0.998 until $n = `r n_star`$. The Q-Q plots show why: even at $n = 30$ the points form visible horizontal steps, because the sample mean can only be $0, 1/30, 2/30, \dots$ and a lot of samples tie at the same values.

So for this population there are really two separate problems: skewness (which theory handles well) and discreteness (which theory based on moments doesn't capture at all).

## What surprised me?

I didn't expect the binomial to end up needing about as large an $n$ as the exponential, or even larger, since its skewness is a lot smaller. The discreteness ended up mattering more than I thought. I also noticed that at $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ the histogram barely looks like it changes, since with $p = 0.1$ nearly every sample is just a bunch of zeros and ones.

```{r}
#| label: save
save_results("Binomial Small (5, 0.1)", tab, n_star,
             "Skewness fine by ~30 but discreteness keeps Q-Q plot stair-stepped")
```
